takes.text: This chip has over twenty thousand cores.
And not one of them can think for itself.
That's exactly why it's so fast.
A CPU is built for decisions.
A few brilliant cores, each spending most of its silicon on prediction, caching, and control — to finish one task as fast as possible.
A GPU makes the opposite bet.
It strips most of that cleverness out, and spends the silicon on raw arithmetic — copied thousands of times.
It doesn't even run your program. The CPU does.
It copies your data into the GPU's memory, then sends one small function, with a single order: run this, a million times.
Zoom into the chip, and you find one block, stamped out again and again.
NVIDIA calls it a streaming multiprocessor. AMD, a compute unit.
A flagship card has a hundred and seventy.
Each copy of that function is a thread.
Threads are packed into blocks; each block lands on one unit, which slices it into squads of thirty-two, called warps.
Here's the trick: a warp shares one instruction stream.
Each instruction is fetched once… then all thirty-two threads execute it together, each on its own data.
Like a rowing crew: one call, thirty-two oars.
So those twenty thousand cores aren't tiny CPUs.
They're lanes of arithmetic, marching in lockstep.
Inside each unit, a scheduler juggles dozens of warps.
Every thread keeps its registers right on the chip — so when one warp stalls on memory, another takes over instantly. Zero cost.
And they stall on memory a lot.
Registers are instant. A small shared scratchpad lets threads in a block trade results. Then caches.
Then VRAM — feeding a flagship chip over a thousand gigabytes every second.
And often, that's still the real speed limit.
Now it clicks.
A 4K frame is eight million pixels, each running the same small program on different data. Perfect.
A neural network is mostly giant matrix multiplications: billions of identical multiply-adds. Also perfect.
But make threads disagree — half branch left, half right — and half the squad sits idle while the others work.
Make them wait on each other, and the lanes go quiet.
So a GPU isn't a faster CPU.
It's a machine for doing one thing to an ocean of data, all at once.
Give it that, and it's unstoppable.
Give it anything else… and your CPU still wins.
